review: Get ready to be highly annoyed by this little tractor beam platformer.

*Radium*, developed by Lukas Jaeckel and published by Develobster, is a tightly focused physics-based challenge that builds its entire experience around precision and control. It does not rely on narrative, spectacle, or layered systems to hold attention; instead, it leans into a stripped-down design where every moment is about mastering a single, unusual way of moving through space. This minimalist approach gives the game a clear identity, one that feels both refreshing and demanding depending on the player’s expectations.

The defining feature is its control system, which replaces direct movement with force-based interaction. Players guide a small sphere using two beams that push and pull it across each level, creating motion indirectly rather than through traditional inputs. This immediately sets the game apart, as movement feels less like steering and more like manipulating momentum. Early on, this can feel awkward or unintuitive, but as players begin to understand how the forces interact, the system reveals a surprising level of depth. Learning to control speed, direction, and positioning becomes the central challenge, and even small improvements in technique can make a noticeable difference.

Level design is built around this mechanic, with each stage acting as a focused test of specific skills. Early levels introduce basic concepts in a manageable way, gradually building toward more demanding scenarios that require precise timing and careful planning. Obstacles such as tight corridors, hazards, and shifting environmental rules push players to refine their approach, often requiring multiple attempts to succeed. The inclusion of mechanics like altered gravity or polarity changes adds variety, forcing players to rethink how movement works under different conditions.

What makes *Radium* engaging is how it emphasizes mastery over progression. There are no character upgrades or external systems to rely on; improvement comes entirely from the player’s ability to better understand and control the mechanics. This creates a strong sense of accomplishment when difficult levels are completed, as success feels directly tied to skill rather than to accumulated advantages. At the same time, this design can be unforgiving, as there are few safety nets for players who struggle with precision-based gameplay.

Visually, the game adopts a clean and minimal style that prioritizes clarity. Levels are composed of simple shapes and contrasting colors, ensuring that players can easily read the environment and focus on movement. This approach supports the gameplay effectively, but it also means that visual variety is limited. Over extended sessions, the environments can begin to feel repetitive, as the aesthetic remains largely consistent throughout the game.

The pacing reflects its challenge-oriented design. Levels are short and can be completed quickly, but repeated attempts are often necessary, especially as difficulty increases. This creates a loop of experimentation and refinement that can be highly satisfying for players who enjoy skill-based challenges. However, the repetition inherent in this process may not appeal to everyone, particularly those looking for a more varied or narrative-driven experience.

Replayability is centered on improvement and efficiency. Players can revisit levels to refine their performance, achieve better completion times, or simply test their mastery of the mechanics. While the game does not introduce significant new content beyond its initial structure, the challenge of perfecting each level provides ongoing motivation for those who enjoy pushing their limits.

In the end, *Radium* succeeds by staying focused on what it does best. It offers a distinctive take on movement and control, supported by carefully designed challenges that reward precision and persistence. While its minimalist approach may limit its appeal to a broader audience, it provides a satisfying and engaging experience for players who appreciate games built around skill and mastery rather than variety or spectacle.

Rating: 7/10

"Radium" ist ein Casual Geschicklichkeits-Puzzle-Spiel mit Zeitlimit.

Das Prinzip ist simpel: wir müssen eine grüne Kugel durch ein Labyrinth zum Endpunkt bugsieren. Problem dabei: wir kontrollieren die Kugel nicht direkt. Das Einzige was uns zur Verfügung steht sind zwei fixierte Beeinflusser, die eine Art Magnetwirkung auf dir Kugel ausüben. Wir können eines oder beide aktivieren. Da die Kugel auch physikalisch auf Schwerkraft reagiert und auch leicht gummiartig zu hüpfen imstande ist, können wir sie mit diesem System recht elegant zu ihrem Ziel führen.

Im Verlauf der 130 Level kommen noch diverse Schwierigkeiten hinzu. Ein eingeschränktes Sichtfeld etwa oder eine Umkehrung der Schwerkraft, Spitzen, die unsere Kugel zerstören oder Flächen, die erstmal aktiviert werden müssen, bevor man den Endbereich aktivieren kann.

Das Ganze ist so wie ein gutes Casual-Spiel sein soll: ein simples Spielprinzip umgesetzt in kreativen Aufgaben. Und es macht Spaß, eine Menge sogar, wäre da nicht der schnell steigende Schwierigkeitsgrad. Wobei auch der nicht so ein großes Problem wäre, herausfordernd soll es ja auch sein, aber: die Zeitvorgabe, die jedes Level hat wird schnell nervig. An sich kann man sich zwar soviel Zeit lassen wie man will, um einen einzelnen Level zu lösen, um weiter Level freizuschalten, muß man allerdings eine bestimmte Anzahl vorheriger Level innerhalb des sehr engen Zeitlimits schaffen. 

Das führt zu Frust, insbesondere bei Spielern wie mir, der zwar gute Rätsel mag, sich aber nur ungern bei der Lösung selbiger hetzen läßt. Wen das nicht stört oder wer den Druck sogar mag, findet hier ein mechanisch sauberes und richtig gut durchdachtes Spielchen.

Grafisch und soundtechnisch ist das Game extrem reduziert, was aber durchaus zum Genre paßt und ästhetisch angemessen wirkt.

Radium is a game based on your skill to navigate a ball through hazardous environments, by controlling the ball with two control points that exert force on the ball. Some levels include collecting tokens to open the exit. You should watch that short video on the store page, screenshots can't depict how the interaction with the ball works.

It's very simple, and I found it challenging in exactly the right way. Difficult, but not frustrating. Getting a feel for the physics, retrying and learning the levels is a big element, and you will make progress and it feels very rewarding. There are no random elements in this game, when you fail it will be your fault and you will happily try again. The experience is very smooth, with a very short 2 seconds countdown before the timer starts, and a key that instantly restarts the level if you're about to fail. The levels are quite short, rarely more than a minute long, most of them around 30 seconds I guess.

Then there are time limits to beat to collect stars, and this game becomes essentially a racing game where you have to take corners with the right amount of speed, you will steer and drift and use walls or try other approaches through parts of a level, to try and optimize your time. 

There are several gameplay mechanics that the game employs to change things up and keep you entertained (very successfully so, I might add):
- collecting tokens: in some levels, they are distributed around a maze or nonlinear network of tunnels that you have to learn or to optimize your path through them. In other levels they just are scattered in an open area with some hazards, and you have to see how to collect them quickly by just steering the ball as precise as possible around the hazards. You'll often have to weigh risk of collisions against speed.
- special tokens that reverse the ball control, from pulling towards the control points to pushing away from the control points. Often they cannot be bypassed and you have to be ready to adapt to that other "mode", which is always a chance for disaster :)
- limited visibility in some levels: sometimes there's darkness and only your ball's surroundings are illuminated to some extent, which emphasizes your learning the level, with each retry getting better and anticipating the point where to break or where to initiate a curve or something. Like car racing in fog, on a track you are familiarizing yourself with. Some maze levels employ this limited visibility to make you try out branches of paths, and to beat a certain time limit you'll have to remember and take the direct path to the exit.
- many of the later levels have moving hazards (for example sawblades) that follow a path, and timing your movements and controlling the speed of the ball becomes even more important. Things can get tight and you have to be quite precise in controlling the ball. The movements of those hazards are predetermined and never random, so retrying a level will eventually help you master it.

Most of the levels have a very nice difficulty, I rarely spent more than 20 minutes on single level until I was able to beat the hardest time limit to earn 3 stars. Often it was more like 3 minutes. But it's not easy either, it's very normal to initially fail a level a couple of times by colliding with a hazard, or to make it through but not beating any time limit and thus earning only 1 star.

I noticed that within most levels the most challenging/risky parts of that level come up near the level beginning, which is a player-friendly way of designing things because this way you're not wasting time on any part that leads to the risky part where failure is probable. I've seen other games make that mistake but Radium keeps you motivated to retry, and keeps boredom low. There are some exceptions in the last levels though.

For people who care about achievements and 100%ing their games: this game is absolutely friendly in this regard, the later levels pose a challenge but it's not a matter of luck but a matter of skill, there are no broken achievements and the achievements are not grindy.

Radium is a puzzle game where you have to go through obstacles to reach the end of the level. If you complete a level in a certain time period, you will receive three "stars". Those stars are used to unlock more sections/levels. During the beginning of the game, the levels are pretty easy and are a bit boring. As you progress through the game, the levels gradually become more and more difficult, so difficult you would either smash your keyboard or throw your mouse at the wall. If you like a challenging mind game or any kind of puzzle game, Radium is the perfect game for you. If you are more into FPS games you probably would find it quite uninteresting and would not enjoy Radium as much as others. Nevertheless, this is a great game where you can spend hours trying to complete a level with three stars.
10/10 would throw my mouse again.

It's something of a new concept but as puzzle games go, you can do much better. The level design is dull and it possesses points that if you don't do perfectly, you have to restart. There's enough ideas to fill a game about a quarter of the length, so much of it is repeated ad-nauseum.

It's worth the price if you're intrigued by the concept, but if you just want a puzzle game to entertain the mind, there are better games for a similar price.
